title: ESP32 IoT Basics: Sensors, Wi-Fi, and Dashboards
learning_objectives: Explain IoT architecture (sensor, controller, network, dashboard)
Connect an ESP32 to Wi-Fi in station mode
Read a sensor and serve the value over HTTP
Identify security and privacy considerations for IoT devices
introduction: The Internet of Things connects physical devices to a network so their data can be monitored and acted on remotely. An ESP32 microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi can read sensors and serve data to a browser dashboard — turning a phone or laptop into a remote display.
real_world_application: Smart homes, environmental monitoring, industrial automation, and wearable devices all use IoT. An ESP32 sensor node can report temperature, humidity, or air quality to a dashboard anywhere on the network.

core_concepts.definition: A network of physical devices that collect and exchange data over the internet or local network.
A device that measures physical quantities and transmits data.
A device that connects sensor nodes to the internet or cloud.
The ESP32 connects to an existing Wi-Fi network as a client.
The ESP32 creates its own Wi-Fi network for direct device connection.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — how browsers request and receive web pages.
Message Queuing Telemetry Transport — a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol for IoT.
A web interface that displays sensor data and device status.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Connect the ESP32 to your computer via USB.
2. Write code to connect to Wi-Fi using WiFi.begin(ssid, password).
3. Wait for connection: while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) delay.
6. In loop(): check for client connections, read sensor, respond with HTML.
7. Open the ESP32's IP address in a browser to see the dashboard.
8. For MQTT: connect to a broker, publish sensor data to a topic, subscribe to control topics.
wiring_instructions: Connect DHT11 data pin to an ESP32 GPIO (e.g., pin 4). Connect VCC to 3.3 V, GND to GND. Add a 10 kO pull-up resistor on the data line if not built into the module.
diagram_specification: ESP32 connected to DHT11 sensor. ESP32 connected to Wi-Fi router. Browser on laptop/phone accesses ESP32 IP address.

code_examples.explanation: ESP32 joins Wi-Fi, reads DHT11, and serves an HTML page with the latest values to any connected browser.

line_by_line_code_explanation: WiFi.begin(ssid, pass) — connects to the Wi-Fi network.
WiFi.localIP() — prints the assigned IP address to Serial Monitor.
server.begin() — starts the web server on port 80.
server.available() — checks for incoming client connections.
client.println() — sends HTTP response to the browser.

interactive_experiment.description: Simulate sensor data flowing from an ESP32 to a dashboard.
interactive_experiment.expected_behavior: Changing sensor values updates the dashboard display. Connection state affects data flow.

expected_observations: ESP32 connects to Wi-Fi and gets an IP address.
Browser can access the IP address and see sensor values.
Values update when the page is refreshed.
If Wi-Fi disconnects, the dashboard shows stale or no data.
common_mistakes: Using 5 GHz Wi-Fi (ESP32 only supports 2.4 GHz).
Wrong SSID or password (connection fails silently).
Not checking WiFi.status() before starting the server.
Reading sensor too frequently (DHT11 needs 2 s between reads).
Not closing the client connection (causes memory leaks).
troubleshooting_steps: Cannot connect to Wi-Fi: verify SSID/password, ensure 2.4 GHz network.
Page won't load: find the IP address in Serial Monitor, ensure same network.
NaN readings: check sensor wiring, add pull-up resistor, wait 2 s after power-on.
Connection drops: check power supply stability, add decoupling capacitor.
safety_notes: Do not expose IoT devices to the public internet without authentication.
Use strong Wi-Fi passwords and consider WPA2/WPA3.
Do not transmit sensitive data without encryption (HTTPS/TLS).
In simulation, no real network or cloud is used.

knowledge_check.question: Which component decides what to do with a sensor reading in an IoT system?
knowledge_check.explanation: The controller (e.g., ESP32) runs the logic that turns readings into decisions.

knowledge_check.question: What does MQTT use to route messages between devices?
knowledge_check.explanation: A broker sits in the middle and forwards messages matching each topic.

mini_challenge: Add a second sensor (light sensor) to the dashboard. Update the HTML to show both readings.
extension_activity: Research MQTT and how to use a broker (like Mosquitto) to connect multiple ESP32 devices.
assumptions: ESP32 with Arduino framework (not ESP-IDF native).
DHT11 sensor with built-in pull-up or external 10 kO resistor.
Single client connection at a time (simple server).
intended_learning_outcome: Learner can connect an ESP32 to Wi-Fi, read a sensor, and serve data to a browser dashboard.
